     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/carbon-dioxide/ and Our World in Data — CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions (Global Carbon Budget 2025)
     5	
     6	## Atmospheric CO₂ Concentration
     7	
     8	The latest measurement from NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory (February 2026) records atmospheric CO₂ at **429 parts per million (ppm)**. This represents a more than 50% increase from the pre-industrial baseline of approximately 280 ppm. The current level is at least 1.5 times greater than the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago — a change that took thousands of years then but has occurred in roughly two centuries now. Ground-based and satellite measurements confirm the sharp acceleration, linked primarily to the burning of coal, oil, and natural gas.
     9	
    10	## Global Emissions Trajectory (1750–2024)
    11	
    12	Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ emissions were negligible. Growth remained relatively slow until the mid-20th century. In **1950**, the world emitted roughly **6 billion tonnes** of CO₂. By **1990**, emissions had nearly quadrupled to over **20 billion tonnes**. Today, global annual emissions from fossil fuels and industry exceed **35 billion tonnes**. While emissions growth has slowed in recent years, they have not yet peaked.
    13	
    14	![Annual CO₂ emissions by country](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    15	
    16	## Who Emits the Most? Country-Level Totals
    17	
    18	China is the world's largest emitter by a significant margin, producing over 12 billion tonnes annually — more than one-quarter of the global total. The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined to roughly 5 billion tonnes. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes. Europe's share has fallen substantially.
    19	
    20	| Country / Region | Approx. Annual CO₂ (billion t) | Share of Global | Trend (recent) |
    21	|---|---|---|---|
    22	| China | ~12.5 | ~27% | Slight increase |
    23	| United States | ~5.0 | ~14% | Declining |
    24	| India | ~3.0 | ~8% | Rising |
    25	| EU-27 | ~2.7 | ~7% | Declining |
    26	| Germany | ~0.6 | ~1.7% | Declining |
    27	| United Kingdom | ~0.3 | ~0.9% | Declining |
    28	| Brazil | ~0.5 | ~1.4% | Roughly stable |
    29	| France | ~0.3 | ~0.8% | Declining |
    30	
    31	In 1900, Europe and the US accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions. Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined.
    32	
    33	## Per Capita Emissions: Extreme Inequalities
    34	
    35	Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The world's highest per capita emitters are major oil-producing nations with small populations (Qatar, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait). Among large, populous countries, the US, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average.
    36	
    37	![Per capita CO₂ emissions over time](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    38	
    39	| Country | Per Capita CO₂ (tonnes/year) |
    40	|---|---|
    41	| United States | ~15 |
    42	| Canada | ~13 |
    43	| Australia | ~15 |
    44	| South Africa | ~8 |
    45	| China | ~9 |
    46	| EU-27 | ~7 |
    47	| World average | ~5 |
    48	| United Kingdom | ~4 |
    49	| France | ~4 |
    50	| India | ~2 |
    51	| Kenya | <1 |
    52	| Chad / Niger | ~0.1 |
    53	
    54	The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately **150-fold**: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year. Importantly, countries with similar living standards can differ significantly — France and the UK have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of their energy mix (higher nuclear and renewable shares).
    55	
    56	## 2024 Annual Change in Emissions
    57	
    58	The 2024 map of annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions shows a mixed picture. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines (roughly −1% to −5%), shown in blue. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more, shown in orange and red. Some countries in South America (notably one or two) experienced very large percentage increases (>10%), while others saw declines.
    59	
    60	![Annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions, 2024](./assets/figure_4.jpg)
    61	
    62	## Key Findings
    63	
    64	- **Global CO₂ emissions now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year** and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth rates.
    65	- **China alone accounts for over 25% of global emissions** (~12.5 Bt), more than double the United States (~5 Bt); India (~3 Bt) is the third-largest and rising fast.
    66	- **The geographic center of emissions has shifted dramatically**: from >90% in Europe and the US in 1900 to Asia producing ~50% today, while the US and Europe combined are below one-third.
    67	- **Per capita inequalities are extreme** — a 150× gap separates the highest emitters (US, Australia at ~15 t/person) from the lowest (Chad, Niger at ~0.1 t/person).
    68	- **Energy mix and policy choices matter**: countries with similar prosperity levels (e.g., France vs. Germany) can have very different per capita emissions depending on their reliance on nuclear, renewables, or fossil fuels.

    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml

# Create 16:9 presentation
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Define a dark, analytical color palette

ACCENT = RgbColor(0x00, 0xC8, 0xFF)   # bright cyan
TEXT_WHITE = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF5, 0xF5)
TEXT_GRAY = RgbColor(0xB0, 0xB8, 0xC8)
MUTED = RgbColor(0x4A, 0x55, 0x6A)

from pptx.oxml.ns import qn

def set_bg_color(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color

# Helper to add textbox
def add_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size, bold=False, color=TEXT_WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name='Calibri'):
    tf = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height).text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.alignment = align
    run = p.runs[0]
    run.font.size = font_size
    run.font.bold = bold
    run.font.color.rgb = color
    run.font.name = font_name
    return tf

# Helper for multi-line textbox
def add_multiline_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, lines, font_size, bold=False, color=TEXT_WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name='Calibri', line_spacing=1.2):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = shape.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = line
        p.alignment = align
        p.space_after = Pt(font_size * (line_spacing - 1))
        run = p.runs[0]
        run.font.size = Pt(font_size)
        run.font.bold = bold
        run.font.color.rgb = color
        run.font.name = font_name
    return tf

# Slide 1: Title

set_bg_color(slide, DARK_BG)

            Pt(44), bold=True, color=TEXT_WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name='Calibri Light')

            Pt(14), bold=False, color=TEXT_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name='Calibri')

shape.fill.solid()
shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT

shape.line.color.rgb = MUTED

prs.save('/app/output/final_deck.pptx')
